I'll work through each draft chapter systematically, applying the gate test strictly and respecting the authorized cuts.

---

**Ch 003 Draft — scan**

The gossip scene is compressed into indirect summary: `"Somebody told me they thought he killed a man once." The girls and Jordan leaned together. "Or that he was a German spy during the war." "Oh, no—he was in the American army," another insisted; and then, with triumphant shiver: "I'll bet he killed a man."`

The source establishes that this exchange is started by one of the Lucille-table girls and includes multiple attributed speakers. Lucille is an authorized cut, so her lines vanishing is expected. The remaining lines read as an odd compressed exchange, but a competent reader can parse it as gossip snatches — not genuinely confusing, just less ornamented. No finding.

The owl-eyes scene is retained in abbreviated form and still parses (Owl Eyes is authorized cut but his scene survives compressed — no seam issue since he is present in the draft text itself). The draft cuts the post-party car wreck entirely, which is an authorized subplot removal. No seam left.

The Jordan driving-conversation is kept. The source's setup is "It was on that same house-party that we had a curious conversation about driving a car. It started because she passed so close to some workmen…" The draft says: `"On a drive together we had a curious conversation."` The source gloss is "same house-party" and the golf-cheating scandal was authorized to be cut, so the "same" loses its referent. But the draft doesn't say "same" — it just says "on a drive together." That parses fine on its own. No finding.

Jordan's dishonesty paragraph: the source links it to the golf-cheating discovery (Warwick house-party, ball moved from bad lie). In the draft the dishonesty paragraph appears *without* the discovery scene — the draft reads: `"The bored, haughty face she turned to the world concealed something—most affectations conceal something eventually, even though they don't in the beginning—and one day I found what it was. Jordan Baker instinctively avoided clever, shrewd men…"` The phrase "one day I found what it was" sets up a revelation, but the revelation (the golf incident) was cut. The pivot "and one day I found what it was" promises a disclosure that never arrives — the very next sentence pivots to her psychology without ever stating what "it" was.

Gate test: a reader is genuinely misled — "one day I found what it was" is a definite promissory clause whose content is never delivered in the draft. The reader is left waiting for the promised finding and it never comes, creating a broken logical structure, not merely a less-ornamented version.

However — is this an authorized cut residue? The authorized cuts include "Jordan Baker's old golf-cheating scandal and Nick's Warwick anecdote (Ch 003)." The seam here is a *direct residue* of that authorized cut. The drafter was told to remove the golf scandal; "one day I found what it was" is the dangling setup that results. Per the instructions, authorized-cut residual seams are NOT findings.

Continuing — no other structural damage found in Ch 003 draft.

---

**Ch 004 Draft — scan**

The timetable passage: `"Once I wrote down, on the empty spaces of a timetable headed 'This schedule in effect July 5th, 1922,' the names of those who came to Gatsby's that summer. They give a better impression than my generalities of those who accepted Gatsby's hospitality and paid him the subtle tribute of knowing nothing whatever about him."` The names themselves are an authorized digression removal, but the draft retains the frame sentence that promises them: "They give a better impression than my generalities." The pronoun "They" refers to names that are never listed. A reader is told a list will provide a better impression, but no list follows — the paragraph simply ends. This is a broken pivot/dangling reference: the sentence exists only as a setup for content that was cut.

Gate test: A reader is genuinely confused — the sentence says "they give a better impression" and then delivers nothing. It reads as a sentence whose main payload was removed, leaving only the introductory framing. This is not merely less ornamented; the sentence's claim becomes false and purposeless without the list.

Is this an authorized cut residue? The authorized digression removal is "Ch 004 — Nick's roll-call catalog of Gatsby's summer guests ('timetable' of names)." The frame sentence was *not* authorized to be cut — only the catalog itself was. The drafter chose to keep the frame while cutting the content it introduces. This is compression damage in surviving material, not a direct residue of the authorized cut itself (which was the list, not the frame). **Valid finding.**

---

The Wolfshiem lunch scene: `"He peered about the room as if he might take one short glance beneath our own table."` In the source, the under-table glance is narrated directly: "I think that, except for my presence, he would have taken one short glance beneath our own table." The draft converts this to a simile ("as if"), which still parses and conveys the meaning. No finding.

`"This is a nice restaurant," Mr. Wolfshiem observed, "but I like across the street better—full of memories."` In the source, Wolfshiem names the Metropole and the Rosy Rosenthal story follows. In the draft, "full of memories" is left without referent content, but the Metropole reminiscence is an authorized digression removal. Residual seam — not a finding.

Gatsby's angry-car-ride confrontation compressed: `"Gatsby leaned toward me. 'I'm afraid I made you a little angry this morning in the car.' I told him I didn't like mysteries and didn't see why Miss Baker must be between us."` This is Nick's speech reported in indirect form; it parses and the substance is clear. No finding.

`"He lifted his cuffs. 'I see you're looking at my cuff buttons.'"` In the source Nick says "I hadn't been looking at them, but I did now." The draft cuts Nick's reaction, so Wolfshiem's statement has no prompt — but this is just compressed narration, and the cuff-button gag still lands. No finding.

Jordan's narration — `"After that winter there were rumours—how her mother had found her one night packing to go to New York…"` The source has "By the next year I had a few beaux myself… She went with a slightly older crowd… Wild rumours were circulating about her—how her mother had found her…" The draft's "After that winter" uses "that winter" as a definite reference. What winter? The preceding draft sentence establishes that Gatsby's encounter with Daisy was "One October day in nineteen-seventeen," then skips to Jordan's brief interaction. No winter has been mentioned in the draft's version of Jordan's narration.

Gate test: "After that winter" uses a definite article for a winter that hasn't been named or established in the draft. However, a competent reader can infer "that winter" means the winter following the autumn 1917 encounter just described. The source's intervening material (Jordan getting beaux, tournaments, Daisy going with older crowd) was cut, but "that winter" in context still points reasonably to the period after the Gatsby-roadster scene. A reader would understand it means the following winter, not be genuinely confused. Not a finding.

`"When I saw them in Santa Barbara she was mad about him. A week after I left, Tom ran into a wagon on the Ventura road and ripped a wheel off his car. The girl with him—a chambermaid at the hotel—got into the papers, too, because her arm was broken."` "The hotel" — which hotel? The source says "one of the chambermaids in the Santa Barbara Hotel." The draft says "a chambermaid at the hotel" — "the hotel" has no explicit antecedent in the draft since "Santa Barbara" was only mentioned as a place ("When I saw them in Santa Barbara") not as "the Santa Barbara Hotel." 

Gate test: Does "the hotel" genuinely confuse a reader? The preceding sentence establishes "Santa Barbara" as the location; "the hotel" in that context is inferable as the hotel in Santa Barbara where they were staying. A competent reader would not be confused — this is a less-precise but parseable reference. Not a finding.

No other structural damage found in Ch 004 draft.
